messages.subject: Degrees of freedom in smoothing splines
messages.subject_clean: Degrees of freedom in smoothing splines
messages.body_plain:
Some days ago I asked a question about degrees of freedom of a spline in
GAM.  I thank Prof. Ripley for his answer, which didn't solve the problem
(the question was rather unclear!).

I have now better identified the problem: when called with argument df,
s(x, ...) and smooth.spline(x, ...) fail to find a curve with the specified
number of degrees of freedom if there are points in x which are "nearly
equal".

Example on S-Plus 4.5 r1:
> x1 <- x2 <- seq(-1, 1, length = 47)[c(1:7,7,7,7,8:47)] # components 7-10
are equal
> x2[7:10] <- x2[7:10] + (-1:2)*1e-4 # components 7-10 are "nearly equal"
> set.seed(317)
> Y <- rnorm(50, x1^2, 0.1) # generating data

> smooth.spline(x1, Y, df = 3)
Call:
smooth.spline(x = x1, y = Y, df = 3)

Smoothing Parameter (Spar): 0.05011098
Equivalent Degrees of Freedom (Df): 3.003106 ### OK!
Penalized Criterion: 1.886019
GCV: 0.02134612

> smooth.spline(x2, Y, df = 3)
Call:
smooth.spline(x = x2, y = Y, df = 3)

Smoothing Parameter (Spar): 0.0004078942
Equivalent Degrees of Freedom (Df): 7.681179 ### wrong!
Penalized Criterion: 0.4356003
GCV: 0.01103843

There is no problem when argument spar is specified:

> smooth.spline(x2, Y, spar = 0.05011)
Call:
smooth.spline(x = x2, y = Y, spar = 0.05011)

Smoothing Parameter (Spar): 0.05011
Equivalent Degrees of Freedom (Df): 3.000345 ### OK!
Penalized Criterion: 1.919406
GCV: 0.02142456

Is this a bug or simply a numerical problem whe have to live with?

Thanks

Pierre Joyet
Baloise Insurance
Switzerland

Um.  Are those empty/blank cells actually blank or are they NULL?  The
look the same in front-ends in general, but they are not the same.

> 1)  Is there any way I can select the data type each column is? In this case
> I'd like to make them strings. I've tried the preview option, and that seems
> to have had no effect.

I assume by `strings' you mean a character vector.  S4 has strings,
so S+6.0 will, but they are different so it is good to not confuse them.

> 2) Why does the factor data type behave this way? Surely if it has no
> observation, it should call that cell an NA (as it would in the case of
> numeric data). 

Surely it is a bug.  When ODBC C code encounters a NULL, it reports
it in a flag and does not change the field.  I've managed to write code
that did this for numeric values too.

As far as I know using "" not NULL in the database avoids this problem.

In addition to the Agresti books already mentioned (which are good) there are

Goodman, L. (1984)  The analysis of cross classified data having ordered

messages.subject: Re: Confusion about least squares
messages.body_plain:
> From: Sicco Schets <Sicco.Schets at asml.nl>
> I am a bit confused about all the different possible functions available
> for linear model fitting and LSQ. I see functions as : lsfit, lm, glm,
> solve, qr.solve (only in R) qr.coef etc.
> 
> I want to use the best method for solving a set of linear equations of
> the form Ax=b, where there are more equations than unknowns. The R
> manual suggests qr.solve. What is the equivalent in S?

A brief tour:

solve: solves equations like Ax=B, where there are as many equations as 
        unknowns, that is A is square and full rank.  (Also can invert A,
        if no B is specified.)

lsfit: least squares regression of B on A, where A is specified as a full-rank
        matrix with more rows than columns.  I think this is what you are
        talking about.  (More commonly in regression, written as Y=Xb+e
        where b is the coefficient vector to be estimated.)

lm: also solves the least squares regression problem, but rather than the 
        user giving the design matrix, it is specified using a model
        formula.  Hence coding of contrasts for categorical variables, 
        calculation of interactions, and so forth are handled automatically.
        Also, the output object contains a lot of additional information
        that can be used with other functions that calculate tests of
        various hypotheses, print results neatly, re-run the regression
        with modified specification, etc.

glm: like lm but more general, fitting a large collection of Generalized
        Linear Models such as logistic regression, Poisson regression, 
        etc.  Can be used for least square regression, but that would be
        overkill.

messages.subject: (Summary) Function that kills S-Plus 2000
messages.body_plain:
I posted a function that kills S-Plus 2000 rel. 3 under NT. Amazingly, I
enticed some people to try it out. Sure enough, it crashes for others, too.
It turns out I've discovered a bug although precisely what the problem is
isn't clear.

Thanks to Patrick Connolly, Henrik Nielsen and Steve McKinney (of
Insightful, formerly MathSoft) for spending time on this.

Patrick Connolly used my function (wittily named death() ) to kill Version
3.4 (Solaris), but, he says, "it doesn't have the whole world crashing down.
Only one process dies.  The emacs session in which I was running Splus is
still there, complete with the text of the function ready to have another
go.  It takes about 3 seconds to be back where I was...it might be worth
your time investigating [emacs and ESS with Windows]"

Henrik Neilsen (using Ver.  5.1 under HP-UX 10.20) noticed that I didn't
have a return value in my function and says, " If I add 'return(ccn)' in the
end of the function I get:

> death()
Problem in prmatrix(x, rowlab = dn[[1.]], collab = c..: collab is wrong
length...

"Before the last assignment [I had]:
> little
 11111 33333 2222222 
     1     1       2
> ccn
 1111111 2222222 3333333 4444444 5555555 
       0       7       0       0       0
> ccn[names(little)]
 1111111 3333333 2222222 
       0       0       7

I am having trouble seeing the logic in this. It seems as if the names are
matched as in the pmatch function?  - Is this documented anywhere?"

A fine question. I will say that the problem does *not* lie in the fact that
the mis-matched names in "little" happen to be shortened versions of the
names in "ccn," because if I replace "11111" and "33333" by "811111" and
"833333," I get another crash.

Steve McKinney from Insightful (they're the people who make S-Plus, by the
way) was abel to replicate my crash on S-Plus 2000 ver. 3 under NT. He notes
that using the function as presented, S-Plus 6.0 beta for Windows doesn't
die. However if he adds ccn as a return value, he gets the same "Problem"
message that Henrik got.
S-PLUS 6.0 beta for windows does not die. "So," Steve says, "something is
amiss internally."

Steve modified death() into the poetically-named phoenix() by replacing the
offending line

ccn[names(little)] <- ccn[names(little)] + little

with 

 ccn[match(names(little), names(ccn), nomatch = 0)] <-
          ccn[match(names(little), names(ccn), nomatch = 0)] +
            little[match(names(ccn), names(little), nomatch = 0)]

and once again the sun shone on the users of S-Plus. Many thanks to all!

Sam ("The S-Plus Slayer") Buttrey
buttrey at nps.navy.mil

-----Original Message-----
From: Buttrey, Samuel [mailto:sebuttre at nps.navy.mil]
Sent: Wednesday, January 31, 2001 4:59 PM
To: 's-news at wubios.wustl.edu'
Subject: [S] function that kills S-Plus 2000

Hi. Here's a cool function that kills S-Plus 2000 rel. 3 running under NT.
What I was trying to do was build up a cumulative table from a bunch of
little tables. I had expected each of the little tables (called "little"
below) to have a subset of the levels in the big table (called "ccn"). I had
forgotten that table() puts the entries in order, so I wanted to prepare for
the case where "little"'s names weren't in the same order as "ccn"'s. The
key is this line:

ccn[names(little)] <- ccn[names(little)] + little

This seems reasonable: increment only the entries of "ccn" which appear as
names of "little." When the names of "little" do indeed form a subset of
those of "ccn," all is well. But in the example below, my whole S-Plus
session crashes, whether I run this inside the function or at the command
line. Is that a little odd? At least once it ran at the command line, doing
vaguely what I expect (which is the creation of new entries of ccn with the
offending names). But from inside a function it crashes every time.

Does anyone dare try it and see what happens? I'd appreciate it: but only do
it if you're prepared to have your whole world come crashing down.

Thanks,

Sam ("The S-Plus Killer") Buttrey
buttrey at nps.navy.mil

> death
function()
{
#
# Death: Program to kill S-Plus 2000 rel. 3 on Windows NT
#
# Create a factor with five levels. Then create the "ccn" table, which has
el
ements
# in only one of these levels.
# 
        ccn.entries <- rep(2222222, 7)
        ccn.labels <- (1:5) * 1111111
        ccn.entries <- factor(ccn.entries, labels = ccn.labels, levels = 
                ccn.labels)
        ccn <- table(ccn.entries)       #
#
# Okay. Now build a "little" table, with three names. One of the three
appear
s among
# the names in "ccn," and the other two don't.
#
        little <- c(11111, 33333, 2222222, 2222222)
        little <- table(little) #
#
# Add the entries of little to the corresponding entries of ccn. And die!
#
        ccn[names(little)] <- ccn[names(little)] + little
}

According to Buttrey, Samuel:

|> I am having trouble seeing the logic in this. It seems as if the names are
|> matched as in the pmatch function?  - Is this documented anywhere?"
|> 
|> A fine question. I will say that the problem does *not* lie in the fact that
|> the mis-matched names in "little" happen to be shortened versions of the
|> names in "ccn," because if I replace "11111" and "33333" by "811111" and
|> "833333," I get another crash.

However, if you replace "11111" and "33333" by the precise equivalents
in your names of ccn, the function works without problem.  It's in
dealing with imprecise matches that it's flakey.  I think you were
interested in precise matches and it's pmatch which is used to subset
that is creating the strange behaviour.  I don't know the whereabouts
of any documentation.

|> Steve modified death() into the poetically-named phoenix() by replacing the
|> offending line
|> 
|> ccn[names(little)] <- ccn[names(little)] + little
|> 
|> with 
|> 
|>  ccn[match(names(little), names(ccn), nomatch = 0)] <-
|>           ccn[match(names(little), names(ccn), nomatch = 0)] +
|>             little[match(names(ccn), names(little), nomatch = 0)]
|> 
|> and once again the sun shone on the users of S-Plus. Many thanks to all!

That will return a ccn of

 1111111 2222222 3333333 4444444 5555555 
       0       9       0       0       0

which is what Sam was aiming at (I think).

Abdulkadir Hussein's idea of introducing a temp object will make ccn
into

 1111111 2222222 3333333 4444444 5555555 
       1       9       1       0       0
which I don't think is desirable.  Imprecise matching has some fishhooks.

Students of Comparative Software, S languages will note that the
matching is done precisely in R.  The original death() function will
return a ccn 

 1111111 2222222 3333333 4444444 5555555   11111   33333 
       0       9       0       0       0                 

without any fiddling with the default matching method.  Just what to
make of the empty bits at the end could be an interesting question,
depending on what the original objective was.

I would be interested in knowing what Splus 6 returns, since something
has evidently been changed.  Maybe it is now 'not unlike R'. :-)

best

messages.subject: survival analysis
messages.body_plain:
SPLUS 2000 NT

Imagine that a data set has survival times recorded for patients in 48 
hospitals.  There are between 10 and 2000 patients per hospital.  There are 
additionally 3 two level factors and 1 three level factor, each assigned in 
a factorial manor to hospitals, such there are 24 treatment 
combinations.  Each treatment combination is assigned to 2 hospitals 
randomly. The patients are successfully followed for 45 years.

Alternatively, there are survival times recorded for soil mites in 48 
tubes.  There are between 10 and 2000 mites per tube intitially (density 
matters).  3 two level factors and 1- three level factor = 24 treatments, 
replicated twice to get the 48 tubes. The mite event history is known for 
45 days.

Individuals within a tube are highly correlated... from a glm perspective, 
using individuals in tubes would be pseudo replication, b/c the treatments 
are assigned to tubes (hospitals)

Is it appropriate to consider individuals as the unit for survival 
analysis, when in effect they are nested in tube/hospital?

When should tube/hospital be a factor?

Can it be justified to analyze each tube/hospital and then use the median 
(or other percentile) as a dependent variable in a GLM framework.

cheers
andrew

messages.subject: Re: suppressing features from densityplot
messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 2 Feb 2001, Edward Malthouse wrote:

> Dear S-news readers,
>
> I would like to suppress the stripplot (row of dots showing
> individual values of variable) that appear at the bottom of a
> density estimate.  I've checked the man pages for densityplot,
> panel.densityplot, and trellis.args without any luck.

You need to write a special panel function.  Just do

panel.dp <- panel.densityplot
fix(panel.dp)  # delete the last line
densityplot( ~ height | voice.part, data = singer, layout = c(2, 4),
            panel=panel.dp, aspect= 1, xlab = "Height (inches)", width = 5)

> I'd also like to suppress the values/tick marks on the vertical
> axis (for a particular audience I'd rather not have to explain what
> they mean).  With plot, I'd use yaxt="n", but this doesn't seem to
> have any effect with densityplot.

Use the scales argument from trellis.args. Adding the argument
scales=list(y=list(draw=F)) does what you want.

--

messages.subject: repeat
messages.body_plain:
Dear s-plus users:

 I have a function to calculate weights and distances under certain
conditions as the followings:

s<-0.6
w<-1/(sqrt(pi)*s)*(exp(-d^2/(2*31.59*s^2)))
w9<-matrix(w,250,250)
w11<-w9[1,1:250]/sqrt(sum(w9[1:250,1]^2))

i<-2
  while (i<251) {
w11<-append(w11,w9[1:250,i]/sqrt(sum(w9[1:250,i]^2)))
i<-i+1
}
w2<-matrix(w11,250,250)

c2<-matrix(c1,250,1)
c3<-t(c2) %*% (w2)
max(c3)

 where c1 is original data(250 cases), and both d and w are 250 by 250
matrix. It works fine, but my purpose is to repeat it for a range of s
value(0.6 to 2.5) and compare it with max(c3) values. The above one
produces one maximum c3 value, but I want to get 20 different s values and
the corresponding max(c3) values so that I can plot those values.

 I've tried several ways to repeat it, but it doesn't work well. I think
complex structure(large matrix, several variables) makes it difficult to
loop or put counter on it. When I try append the matrix for repeat, I've
got some allocation error because the matrix exceeds maximum object size
limit. I wonder whether there are more efficient ways to do it. 
 Any help would be appreciated. 
 Thank you.

Daikwon Han

On 1 Feb 2001, at 9:05, Buttrey, Samuel wrote:

> I posted a function that kills S-Plus 2000 rel. 3 under NT. Amazingly, I
> enticed some people to try it out. Sure enough, it crashes for others, too.
> It turns out I've discovered a bug although precisely what the problem is
> isn't clear.
> 
> Thanks to Patrick Connolly, Henrik Nielsen and Steve McKinney (of
> Insightful, formerly MathSoft) for spending time on this.
> 
> Patrick Connolly used my function (wittily named death() ) to kill Version
> 3.4 (Solaris), but, he says, "it doesn't have the whole world crashing down.
> Only one process dies.  The emacs session in which I was running Splus is
> still there, complete with the text of the function ready to have another
> go.  It takes about 3 seconds to be back where I was...it might be worth
> your time investigating [emacs and ESS with Windows]"
> 
> Henrik Neilsen (using Ver.  5.1 under HP-UX 10.20) noticed that I didn't
> have a return value in my function and says, " If I add 'return(ccn)' in the
> end of the function I get:
> 
> > death()
> Problem in prmatrix(x, rowlab = dn[[1.]], collab = c..: collab is wrong
> length...
> 
> "Before the last assignment [I had]:
> > little
>  11111 33333 2222222 
>      1     1       2
> > ccn
>  1111111 2222222 3333333 4444444 5555555 
>        0       7       0       0       0
> > ccn[names(little)]
>  1111111 3333333 2222222 
>        0       0       7
> 
> I am having trouble seeing the logic in this. It seems as if the names are
> matched as in the pmatch function?  - Is this documented anywhere?"
> 
> A fine question. I will say that the problem does *not* lie in the fact that
> the mis-matched names in "little" happen to be shortened versions of the
> names in "ccn," because if I replace "11111" and "33333" by "811111" and
> "833333," I get another crash.
> 
> 
> Steve McKinney from Insightful (they're the people who make S-Plus, by the
> way) was abel to replicate my crash on S-Plus 2000 ver. 3 under NT. He notes
> that using the function as presented, S-Plus 6.0 beta for Windows doesn't
> die. However if he adds ccn as a return value, he gets the same "Problem"
> message that Henrik got.
> S-PLUS 6.0 beta for windows does not die. "So," Steve says, "something is
> amiss internally."
> 
> Steve modified death() into the poetically-named phoenix() by replacing the
> offending line
> 
> ccn[names(little)] <- ccn[names(little)] + little
> 
> with 
> 
>  ccn[match(names(little), names(ccn), nomatch = 0)] <-
>           ccn[match(names(little), names(ccn), nomatch = 0)] +
>             little[match(names(ccn), names(little), nomatch = 0)]
> 
> and once again the sun shone on the users of S-Plus. Many thanks to all!
> 
> Sam ("The S-Plus Slayer") Buttrey
> buttrey at nps.navy.mil
> 
> -----Original Message-----
> From: Buttrey, Samuel [mailto:sebuttre at nps.navy.mil]
> Sent: Wednesday, January 31, 2001 4:59 PM
> To: 's-news at wubios.wustl.edu'
> Subject: [S] function that kills S-Plus 2000
> 
> 
> Hi. Here's a cool function that kills S-Plus 2000 rel. 3 running under NT.
> What I was trying to do was build up a cumulative table from a bunch of
> little tables. I had expected each of the little tables (called "little"
> below) to have a subset of the levels in the big table (called "ccn"). I had
> forgotten that table() puts the entries in order, so I wanted to prepare for
> the case where "little"'s names weren't in the same order as "ccn"'s. The
> key is this line:
> 
> ccn[names(little)] <- ccn[names(little)] + little
> 
> This seems reasonable: increment only the entries of "ccn" which appear as
> names of "little." When the names of "little" do indeed form a subset of

On Mon, 5 Feb 2001, Trevor Parker wrote:

> Hello S-plus enthusiasts,
>
>
> I have run a GLM using 2 degree poynomials as independents. The model looks 
> like this:
>
> forest.object <- glm(forest ~ poly(slope,2) + poly(aspectns,2), 
> family=binomial(logit), data=train)
>
> When I use the coefficients from forest.object to predict forest I get 
> erroneous results. i.e very small values
>
> The predictive GLM form I am using is:
>
> log(p/1-p) = intercept + coef1*slope + coef2*sqr(slope) + coef3*aspectns + 
> coef4*sqr(aspectns)
>
> where intercept and coef1 to 4 are from forest.object.
>
> When I run the model:
>
> forest.object <- glm(forest ~ slope + aspectns, family=binomial(logit), 
> data=train)
>
> and use the coefficents to predict forest i.e log(p/1-p) = intercept + 
> coef1*slope + coef2*aspectns
>
> it works well.
>
> I have tried using poly.transform but it appears to only work for models with 
> one independent variable.
>
> Am I using the polynomial form correctly. Your help would be appreciated.

This is well known and well documented. You need to use predict.gam, not
predict.glm.   See for example Venables & Ripley (1999, p.166).

messages.subject: Weighted density estimates
messages.body_plain:
I have data on capital K and profit rates P pertaining to a set of firms X.
S-plus will, of course, easily produce histograms and kernel density
estimates of the distribution of P across X.

However, the theory I am testing makes predictions about the profit rate
distribution weighted by size of capital -- i.e. the probability that a<P<b
is given by sum[Ki/Kt] where the Ki are the amounts of capital employed by
the Xi firms achieving profit rates lying in the interval ab, and Kt is the
total capital employed by all firms.

This is easily worked out and graphed as a histogram in Excel using its PROB
function, but as a beginner I can't see a route to achieving the same result
in S-plus. I'd also like to produce kernel estimates, as well as the

messages.subject: Re: gamma model
messages.body_plain:
B.P. Ripley states, in response to a question by Eric Wong:

BPR> BTW the MLE of the mean of a Gamma glm does not depend on the shape,
BPR> so glm() does fit the MLE for any fixed shape.  What it is does not do is
BPR> to estimate the shape, by MLE or otherwise.

I agree with his predicate, but not the conclusion.  glm() estimates
what its documentation calls the dispersion parameter, abbreviated by
phi, by the Pearson chi-squared statistic divided by the degrees of
freedom.  For a gamma distribution phi is the square of the coefficient
of deviation, or the inverse of the scale parameter nu.  So glm() does
directly estimate the shape of a gamma distribution.

This estimate isn't the MLE.  However, as argued by McCullough and Nelder
(Generalized Linear Models, 2nd Ed., Section 8.3), it is preferable to
the MLE as the latter is not robust.  If you do want the M.L.E. they
provide very easy means to calculate it or approximate it from the
deviance, which is also supplied by glm().

Rick.

You can try to use the following function

try <- function(expr, first = T)
{
# evaluates expr (in frame of caller) and returns either
# its value or the error message (with class "Error").
# DO NOT USE THE 'first' ARGUMENT.
        restart(first)
        if(first) {
                first <- F
                expr
        }
        else {
                error.msg <- get.message()
                class(error.msg) <- "Error"
                error.msg
        }
}

which you call with expr=what you would like to do.

try(solve(matrixA))

Eric

Hi. In recent versions of S-Plus there is a try() function, which works like
the function of the same name in Java. It will catch errors and return them
to you. So your function might look like this:

wang <- function()
{
        bad.matrix <- matrix(0, 2, 2)   # non-invertible
        result <- try(inverse <- solve(bad.matrix))
        cat ("We got here successfully!\n")
        invisible (return(result))
}

Then when you call it, you trap the error:

> out <- wang ()
Error in solve.qr(a): apparently singular matrix  # <- Error message still
prints to screen: don't worry
We got here successfully!                              # Here's where you
can handle your error

> out    # Look at return value
[1] "Error in solve.qr(a): apparently singular matrix\n"
attr(, "class"):
[1] "Error"

Does this help?

Whoever that is?

> BPR> BTW the MLE of the mean of a Gamma glm does not depend on the shape,
> BPR> so glm() does fit the MLE for any fixed shape.  What it is does not do is
> BPR> to estimate the shape, by MLE or otherwise.
>
> I agree with his predicate, but not the conclusion.  glm() estimates
> what its documentation calls the dispersion parameter, abbreviated by
> phi, by the Pearson chi-squared statistic divided by the degrees of
> freedom.  For a gamma distribution phi is the square of the coefficient
> of deviation, or the inverse of the scale parameter nu.  So glm() does
> directly estimate the shape of a gamma distribution.

so I was correct all along. It is summary.glm() that does.  You need to
read the code more carefully (as well as people's names).

> (Generalized Linear Models, 2nd Ed., Section 8.3), it is preferable to
> the MLE as the latter is not robust.  If you do want the M.L.E. they
> provide very easy means to calculate it or approximate it from the
> deviance, which is also supplied by glm().

examples in the on-line complements to the book.

On Tue, 6 Feb 2001, Xiaofei Wang wrote:

>

> could be singular. However, once the inverse is failed, Splus will stop
> abruptly, give error message and discard everything from previous
> simulation.
> 
> My question is how to keep Splus going even when the inverse is failed.

You can use the try() function to keep going after an otherwise
fatal error.  If you suspect that
        z <- f(x,y)
might fail then replace it with
        z <- try(f(x,y))
        if (inherits(z, "Error")) {
                ... deal with error ...
        } else {
                ... z now has the value of f(x,y) ...
        }
try(expression) returns the value of the expression if it succeeded
and returns an object of class "Error" containing the error message
if it failed.

> If I need to check singularity before doing inverse, what is a good way to do
> the checking.

You could look at the singular values (from svd()) but it might
be easiest to use try().

RC> B.P. Ripley states, in response to a question by Eric Wong:

BPR> Whoever that is?

Eric Wong was the person I took to be the originator of the thread.
B.P. Ripley is a statistician noted for technical expertise and 
lack of social graces.

A few comments on the subject, which was the estimation of shape
parameters by glm().  One does need to summarize the object created by glm()
in order to get this explicitly computed: summary(glm()) has a component
called $dispersion.

Another issue, which wasn't raised but which is potentially important
(I learned the hard way) is to use the correct distribution in an
analysis of deviance given by the anova() function.  The test="F"
option is appropriate when the dispersion parameter is estimated and
the test="Chi" option is suitable for models in which it is set to
one.  They can yield quite different output.

Rick.

messages.body_plain:
Hi, everybody,

I would like to thank all persons who responded my question about how to
keep Splus going after a failure in inverting a singular matrix. They are
Eric Lecoutre,Samuel Buttrey, Bill Dunlap, Matt Kurbat, Prof. Brian
Ripley, Alan Zaslavsky and Jingli Song. Their expertise and kindness has
made this mailing list such a great community.

In case anybody else has a similar question, I documented their
suggestions here.

There are three kinds of solutions:

1. Use try() function in Splus to catch the error 
   Suggested by Eric Lecoutre,Samuel Buttrey, Bill Dunlap,Matt Kurbat,
Prof Brian Ripley

One example provided by Bill Dunlap illustrates how to use try() to catch
the error.

Example

       z <- try(f(x,y))
        if (inherits(z, "Error")) {
                ... deal with error ...
        } else {
                ... z now has the value of f(x,y) ...
        }
}

(2) Check singularity before inverting a matrix 
    Suggested by Alan Zaslavsky

There are several methods to check singularity. One of them is to use
qr() and see if the rank component indicates that the matrix is less than
full rank. It is easy to add this check within the function solve().

Example

solve.default <- function(a, b)
{
    if(!(missing(b) || is.numeric(b) || mode(b) == "complex"))
        stop("b must be numeric or complex")
    if(!is.list(a))
        a <- qr(a)
    if(missing(b))
        solve.qr(a)
    else solve.qr(a, b)
}

(3) Use generalized inverse function ginverse()
   Suggested by Jingli Song

His solution is similar to (2). Use ginverse() instead of solve() and
check the rank of the inverse to decide if singularity occurs.

Example

a<-matrix(c(2,0,0,2),2,2)
solve(a)
     [,1] [,2]
[1,]  0.5  0.0
[2,]  0.0  0.5
ginverse(a)
     [,1] [,2]
[1,]  0.5  0.0
[2,]  0.0  0.5
attr(, "rank"):
[1] 2

Please refer to their original messages attached below for detail.

Cheers,

Xiaofei Wang
Graduate Student in Biostatistics
Univ. of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

==================================================================

messages.subject: Re: gamma model
messages.body_plain:
The topic, if we can rise above the flames, is an interesting one in
general.

The original question addressed the issue of estimating dispersion
parameters in generalized linear models.  This is done via summary(),
which in turn invokes summary.glm(), operating on results produced
from glm().  The estimate isn't an MLE but a Pearson statistic.
McCullagh and Nelder give good reasons to choose the latter for a gamma
distribution but don't say anything about the loss of efficiency.  Does
anyone have any ideas on this?

A related issue is when to estimate the (over)dispersion parameter for
binomial and Poisson distributions or, more properly, when to use such
an estimate in inference about the mean.  For very small class sizes in
the binomial, I would think it is too variable to be of use.  For very
large class sizes I would use the estimate to adjust p-values and
confidence intervals.  But for the general case, I don't have a sense.
Anyone need a thesis topic?  Or have I missed one which has already been
done (I know about Liang and McCullagh's nice case study in Biometrics
49, pp. 623-630, 1993)?

Jean-Baptiste DENIS writes:
J-BD> If the quotation is true, I would appreciate an answer from Rick Chappell.

A few people have criticized me in the newsgroup for this (and about a
dozen have agreed with me by e-mail, an interesting case of selection
bias), so I suppose I ought to reply:

The quotation, which was:

RC|> Eric Wong was the person I took to be the originator of the thread.
RC|> B.P. Ripley is a statistician noted for technical expertise and
RC|> lack of social graces.

is certainly true in the sense that I wrote it.  Whether its content
is accurate, except for the middle initial, those who care can judge.

I have been participating, usefully I believe and hope, in this list
from its inception and these five words constitute the first which can
remotely be considered a flame.

I have seen a great many cases in which B.D. Ripley gave valuable
technical advice.  But I have also seen too many replies in which he
was quite rude to me and many others in response to items as trivial as
mispellings.   This includes posters whose primary language is not
English.  Yes, after a certain point, I am not averse to asking anyone
to mind his manners.

Now does anyone have any opinions on my technical comments?

Rick Chappell.

| -----Original Message-----
| From: jingshan zhang [mailto:jszhang at stat.rutgers.edu]
| Sent: Thursday, 8 February 2001 7:19
| To: s-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu
| Subject: [S] Is there a good way to carry out this faster?
| 
| 
| Hi, all:
| 
| I have to compute the trimmed means of all columns in 
| a 20x10000 matrix. I have tried the following:
| 
| apply(X,2,mean,trim=.1) where X is the large matrix.
| It will take about 16 seconds. Can someone suggest a 
| way to make it faster?

Not without essentially doing the trimming by hand.  Here is one way you
could consider.  Let's start with a sample that will probably need trimming:

> X <- matrix(rcauchy(200000), 20, 10000)

Now let's see how fast your method is on my slow machine:

> dos.time(xb <- apply(X, 2, mean, trim = 0.1))
[1] 20.27997

Here is a way of doing it by hand.  The idea is to do all the sorting in one
move using order() and do all the trimming and meaning in one matrix
operation.  
The code below modifies the X matrix, but that could easily be avoided:

> dos.time({

+ X[] <- X[order(rep(1:10000, each=20), X)]     # sort
+ xb0 <- as.vector(rep(1/16, 16) %*% X[3:18, ]) # trim & mean

+ })
[1] 3.340027

Not bad, but if you are only going to be doing it once you will spend more
time on typing than anything else.  This is only useful if you are going to
be doing it plenty of times.  (You might like to sort out why it works.)

Oh, did we get the same answer each time?  Well:

> range(xb-xb0)
[1] -5.551115e-016  4.440892e-016
> 

Not bad.

messages.subject: coding efficiency (incls SUMMARY: polychoric correlations)
messages.body_plain:
All

Many thanks to Jari Haukka and Michael Bramley  who
responded to my question on polychoric correlations. 
Dr Haukka sent me a C program by Scott M. Lynch (which
I have not included below - contact me if you want
it).  I have not tried it myself at this stage. 
Michael Bramley informed me that a friend is working
on code but it is not ready yet.

Before these responses came through, I got round to
creating my own rough, ready and crude S+ code - the
full function is at the bottom of this email.  I am
now interested in the exercise of improving my code as
a learning experience and interesting in its own
right.

The function .polychoric.2way produces the correct
answer with test data but it does it so slowly
(S+2000, Pentium III, 128MB) that it is painful to
watch.  I'd be interested in any advice on how to get
rid of the nasty nested loops in the middle of my
function .polychoric.2way, or otherwise speed up the
function.  

The aim of the offending code is to calculate and
iteratively maximise a likelihood function which is
the sum of the following function in each cell in an i
by j contingency table where a and b are vectors of
thresholds which have been calculated previously:

F(a [i], b [j]) - F(a [i-1], b [j])
 - F(a [i], b [j-1]) + F(a [i-1], b [j-1])

and where F is a cumulative bivariate normal
distribution function with correlation rho, which is
the parameter we are seeking to maximise over.  As an
exercise in brute, crude strength, I coded this as an
ugly function fed to nlmin, with repeated calls to
pmvnorm.  As you will see, I also encountered problems
with pmvnorm not liking to give the cumulative
distribution of an infinite argument, around which I
built another ugly workaround.

Any ideas from cleverer and more expert heads for more
elegant solutions gratefully received.

My test session is here:

> test <- matrix(c(58,26,8,52,58,12,1,3,9),3,3)
> .polychoric.2way(test, tab=T) # tab=T needed
$r:
[1] 0.4199

$threshA:
[1] -0.02761  1.13708

$threshB:
[1] -0.2397  1.5781

Warning messages:
  NAs generated in: log(P)
> dos.time(.polychoric.2way(test, tab=T))
[1] 73.25
Warning messages:
  NAs generated in: log(P)

And the actual function are below my signature.

TIA

PE

Peter Ellis
Curtin University

.polychoric.2way <- function(x, tab = F)
{
#
# takes an n by 2 matrix of 2 ordered factors
# and returns polychoric correlation between the two.
#
# Has option of accepting 2 way contingency 
# table (tab=T).
#
#
# peter_f_ellis at yahoo.com
#
# 3 January 2001
#
        if(!tab) {
                N <- table(x[, 1], x[, 2])
        }
        else N <- x
        ii <- nrow(N)
        jj <- ncol(N)
        Pi <- apply(N, 1, sum)/sum(N)
        Pj <- apply(N, 2, sum)/sum(N)
        a <- qnorm(c(0, cumsum(Pi)))
        b <- qnorm(c(0, cumsum(Pj)))
        r.nlmin <- nlmin(function(rl)
        {
                ii <- get("ii", frame = sys.parent(4))
                jj <- get("jj", frame = sys.parent(4))
                a <- get("a", frame = sys.parent(4))
                b <- get("b", frame = sys.parent(4))
                N <- get("N", frame = sys.parent(4))
                P <- matrix(0, ii, jj)
                for(i in 1:ii) {
                        for(j in 1:jj) {
                                A <- pmvnorm(c(a[i + 1], b[j + 1]), rho = rl * 
((i
!= ii) & (j != jj)))
                                B <- pmvnorm(c(a[i], b[j + 1]), rho = rl * ((i 
!=
1) & (j != jj)))
                                C <- pmvnorm(c(a[i + 1], b[j]), rho = rl * ((j 
!=
1) & (i != ii)))
                                D <- pmvnorm(c(a[i], b[j]), rho = rl * ((i != 
1) &
(j != 1)))
                                P[i, j] <- A - B - C + D
                        }
                }
 - sum(N * log(P))
        }
        , 0)
        if(!r.nlmin$converged) {
                stop("Did not converge")
        }
        r <- r.nlmin$x
        list(r = r, threshA = a[ - c(1, ii + 1)], threshB =
b[ - c(1, jj + 1)])
}

When using the motif() and postscript() devices I have been able to 
display the greek character mu (for "micro") in a graph by using the 
character "\265". For example, mtext('\265g/L') with font=1. This

containing "\265" does not display. There may be some platform and 
version dependencies here, but I have not done exhaustive testing.

Splus is version 6 on Solaris.

one displays the offending text.

Has anyone met this problem before and solved it?

messages.subject: SUM:Poster of S-PLUS graphs
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
     Thanks to all who responded.  Here's my original post:

I'm a new S-PLUS user and I would like to create a poster (3 feet x 3
feet) of the various graphs that I've created in S-PLUS.  Can anyone
suggest a methodology (what output file formats/ software packages) to use?
I ultimately need to create a postscript file that can be sent to our
plotter.  I will summarize and post.

    Here's what has not worked for me:
1) Creating a 3 foot x 3 foot graph sheet in S-PLUS and populating it with
the graphs I had created.  When I did not have the capability to easily
zoom in and around the large graph sheet for proofing, I chose to give
Adobe Illustrator a try - maybe I shouldn't have given up on S-PLUS so
quickly?
2) Exported the 6 graphs individually as .eps files and placed them in
Adobe Illustrator.  Adobe was not able to save as .eps which I wanted.
Adobe also crashed several times as I tried to manipulate the various
graphs.  This behavior was reproduced on 2 other NT machines, even those
with considerable RAM (e.g. 1GB).

There must be a better way....
*******************************************************************************************************************************
Here's a summary of the responses followed by the actual responses.

METHODS:   GETTING MULTIPLE S-PLUS GRAPHS ON A POSTER

wmf ----> MS Powerpoint (set pagesize in custom dimensions)

eps -----> Illustrator ----> save as Illustrator eps ----> Word

eps ----> Adobe PageMaker

eps ----> ImageMagick - manipulate with Montage
       (www.imagemagick.org)

1 eps -----> Illustrator ----> save as native Illustrator format (ai)
      (repeat above step for other eps graph files)
       Combine all 6 ai files in Illustrator

NO File Format Method:
      cut & paste between S-PLUS and Adobe or Corel

*******************************************************************************

From: Ian Jonsen

You could use MS Powerpoint and import S+ graphs as wmf files. You will
need to set the page size in Powerpoint to custom dimensions. The nice
thing about wmf files in MS software is that you can edit them (edit add
color, anotate) after import. Often the line-drawing edit functions in MS
Word / Powerpoint, etc... are better than those in S+.
___________________________

From:  DON MCKENZIE

Adobe does not seem to do well with .eps files created by other
applications.  What has always worked for me is to export a windows
metafile to powerpoint and import it, or several of them, into a slide
with the dimensions appropriate to your poster (since you're using adobe I
assume you're on Windoze).
____________________________

From: Don MacQueen

I have larger posters than yours containing several Splus graphs and
assorted explanatory text. However, I didn't create the poster
myself. I delivered Word files with the text and Splus .eps files to
an Adobe Illustrator expert and he did it.

For your situation, here is what I would try. Take each of the 6 .eps
files and open each one separately, one at a time, in Illustrator.
Save each in a native Illustrator format. Then create a new
Illustrator document and place each of the 6 in it.

In my version of Illustrator there appear to be two "native"
Illustrator formats. They are named "Illustrator" and "Illustrator
EPS". I don't know which you should try, probably the first one.

I frequently open Splus .eps files with Illustrator, save them as
Illustratore EPS, and then import them into a Word document. I've
never had Illustrator crash in this process.

The caveat is that I'm using different versions of everything than
you are. I've done this a lot with Splus v5 on unix (so there's no
such thing as a graph sheet), and Illustrator 8.0.1 on Macintosh.
__________________________

From: S. Byers

Write all the graphs out one by one in the way you normally would with
Splus. Postscript is fine

Then use montage to assemble them into a montage. This is the cleanest and
most flexible way to do what you want. With montage in the ImageMagick
package comes convert, which is also a very useful tool for manipulated
large numbers of images.

www.imagemagick.com
__________________________

From: David Leeth of the USGS

I have done this with both CorelDraw and Adobe.  I typically get the graphs
in "Survey style" within Splus and then cut and paste them into Corel/Adobe
as grouped objects that I can move around and manipulate.  If you have
enough RAM (turn Lotus notes off while doing all of this)  you shouldn't
have any problems cutting and pasting and you can skip all of the
import/export pain and suffering.  If you can't work it out give me a call
__________________________

From: Madeline Bauer

I do this using Adobe PageMaker. I am guessing that PageMaker and
Illustrator probably behave (misbehave) in pretty much the same ways. I
suspect that the problems you are having might be related to (a) the amount
of RAM on your machine and (b) the links options in Illustrator.

Here are a few hints based on my experience:

(a) to maximize the amount of RAM available for Illustrator, do not have
any other program running, including do not have wallpaper or screen saver
programs. Particularly, do not have S-Plus running at the same time.

(b-1) in S-Plus, save the graphs as EPS files, without previews.

(b-2) I scale the layout in PageMaker to 11 x 17 so it is manageable on
screen. Then I send the whole package to a service bureau to get 4' x 8'
poster. Or, you can do the scaling yourself after you're happy with the
layout, by switching printers/PPD files, to the large printer and changing
the scaling option in the print window.

(b-3) in Illustrator, find the links or import options and make sure that
you specify that

[1] the graphics files are not to be saved in the publication and

[2] that you do not want a preview created (also make sure that S-Plus does
not create a preview -- these preview files are huge!)

This does mean that in your Illustrator layout, you will only see a gray
rectangle for each graph. But there are ways around this:

When you want to view the actual output, you should be able to "print" the
publication to a file (in PageMaker, there is an "options" button on the
print window). You can choose to print to an PS or to EPS file. I suggest
that you choose PS.

Alternatively, you should be able to print to your standard postscript
printer by selecting the "shrink to fit" option or the "manual tile"
option.

If you save the file as postscript, you can use GSView to look at it (free
software, ask me how to get it). This saves paper while you iterate until
you are happy with the layout.

If you have Adobe Distiller, you can create Acrobat files from the
postscript output from Illustrator, which is another way to view the output
on screen.

My experience is that PageMaker is like S-Plus. You can get positive
feedback quickly, but there is a relatively steep learning curve to get
what you really want,  but in both cases, it is worth the effort!

Good luck!
Madeline Bauer

PS You can never be too rich or too thin or have too much RAM.
I use Windows 95 and 98, so I do not know about NT, but on 95/98 it is
important to check the Windows settings for the "swap" file.
*******************************************************************

messages.subject: Execution time
messages.body_plain:
Hello S-users,

SPlus-2000 r3, on NT 4.0 sp5

I am lucky enough to run SPlus on a powerfull machine, 1G RAM and dual
processors BUT....

Something has been anoying me for quite some time.  When I work in a work
space holding large objects the most simple task seems to take for ever.
For exemple I am currently in a workspace close to 500M, after I have done
some extensive cleanup, watch the following the following script running:

> ttt.vector <- 1:26
> names(ttt.vector) <- letters
> ttt.time <- proc.time()
>  names(ttt.vector)
 [1] "a" "b" "c" "d" "e" "f" "g" "h" "i" "j" "k" "l" "m" "n" "o" "p" "q" "r" "s"
[20] "t" "u" "v" "w" "x" "y" "z"
> proc.time() - ttt.time
[1] 13.08984

It is taking 13 seconds to get the names of a vector of length 26!!  A very 
long time indeed, I know in that time is included the two
calls to proc.time().  Now let's move to a smaller workspace, roughly 18M

> chdir('glm exemples')
> ttt.vector <- 1:26
> names(ttt.vector) <- letters
> ttt.time <- proc.time()
>  names(ttt.vector)
 [1] "a" "b" "c" "d" "e" "f" "g" "h" "i" "j" "k" "l" "m" "n" "o" "p" "q" "r" "s"
[20] "t" "u" "v" "w" "x" "y" "z"
> proc.time() - ttt.time
[1] 0.3398438

Less than 0.5 sec., same code same machine, same session.  Now if we use the 
little V&R function resources and time it's execution
we find that most of the extra time is spent in wrapping up after the task is 
executed?

> chdir('autoanc')
> resources({ttt.vector <- 1:26
+   names(ttt.vector) <- letters
+   ttt <- names(ttt.vector)})
 CPU Elapsed % CPU Child Cache Working
  NA       0    NA     0  2724       0
> proc.time() - ttt.time
[1] 15.66

It is telling us it took no time, or hardly, to execute the three expressions 
but wrapping up took for ever, almost!  Back to the other
workspace.

> chdir('glm exemples')
> ttt.time <- proc.time()
> resources({ttt.vector <- 1:26
+   names(ttt.vector) <- letters
+   ttt <- names(ttt.vector)})
 CPU Elapsed % CPU Child Cache Working
  NA       0    NA     0     0       0
> proc.time() - ttt.time
[1] 1.619995

Now the wrapping up time is acceptable.

Questions:

   Why this difference?
   Since the nature of my work involves and will keep involving large, very 
large, data sets is there a way to reduce this wrap up time
       or whatever may be causing that?  It seems I spend a lot of my time 
waiting on SPlus, even for very simple tasks?

Any help appreciate,

Gérald Jean
Analyste-conseil (statistiques), Actuariat
télephone            : (418) 835-4900 poste (7639)
télecopieur          : (418) 835-6657
courrier électronique: gerald.jean at spgdag.ca

Hello,

I am using S-Plus 6 for Mandrake Linux and S-PLUS 6 for Windows, Beta
Release 2 on NT4 SerPack6.

This is *not* a post about running out of memory (at least yet).   I am
working with a data set of 2.4 million rows and 5 columns. The machines I
use have plenty of memory (1.5 GB and 2.5 GB RAM for Linux and NT,
respectively), and the calls I make to read-in the data, sort it, and then
process it work to my satisfaction.  (I have worked diligently to follow all
the usual guidelines to manage memory during evaluations.)

My concerns lie with behavior after all evaluations are completed.  I notice
an accumulation of Memory Usage by SPLUS.EXE in the Windows Task Manager and
in Linux with ktop.  I re-mention that this accumulation stays even after
all assignments have been committed, and S-PLUS is idly waiting for more
commands.  I have consulted the standard S-PLUS references: the programmers
manuals, on-line help, V & R, S-news archives, S Poetry, etc. and still am
left curious (perhaps I have not studied hard enough)...

When the data is read-in from a CSV file, the memory usage spikes, settles,
and after completion arrives at a jump of a couple hundred MB.  After the
sort of the data frame with order(), I see similar behavior, and so on with
the data analysis / processing. Under Linux, I learned about the system
command "free", which distinguishes between memory in use and that which is
buffered / cached.  My understanding is that the buffered / cached amount
can be flushed out when the next process in the system needs it.  So under
Linux, I have assured myself that when S-PLUS completes all evaluations &
assignments, that it essentially returns to its initial start-up level of
memory usage (with the exception of cached functions set by default with
options(keep= ) ). 

I am not so assured with Windows of this behavior, though, and I do not have
the knowledge or tools at current to investigate.  (I did try out mem.tally
and allocated functions, but am still unsure if I used them correctly to
answer my question.) I admit to feeling lazy, so I apologize for asking thru
this post if there is any advice that someone could provide.  Essentially,
is there a build-up of memory by S-PLUS that is lost during a session and
thus cannot be used by further S-PLUS evaluations or by other applications?

Many Thanks in advance,
Bill

messages.subject: fitting a normal to a few digitized points?
messages.subject_clean: fitting a normal to a few digitized points?
messages.body_plain:
I am using S+ 2000 R2 on Win98.

I have 1500 dome-shaped curves from a variety of simulations and empirical 
measurements (not mine).  For each curve I digitized the peak and four 
points on each side of the peak at specified proportions (> 50%) of the 
peak height.

I would now like to come up with an approximation for each of my digitized 
curves using a normal distribution, and obtain a measure of how well the 
approximation fits the digitized points (some sort of R2).   The mean of a

messages.subject_clean: fitting a normal to a few digitized points?
messages.body_plain:
Todd Hatfield asks:

| -----Original Message-----
| From: Todd Hatfield [mailto:hatfield at solander.bc.ca]
| Sent: Saturday, 10 February 2001 12:13
| To: s-news at wubios.wustl.edu
| Subject: [S] fitting a normal to a few digitized points?
|
| I am using S+ 2000 R2 on Win98.
| 
| I have 1500 dome-shaped curves from a variety of simulations 
| and empirical measurements (not mine).  

Dome-shaped or bell-shaped?  Most importantly, are they positive and
asymptote to zero in both directions?  This is pretty vital information but
since you talk of a percentage of the peak height, I presume this will be
the case at least notionally.

| For each curve I digitized the peak and four points on each 
| side of the peak at specified proportions (> 50%) of the peak height.
| 
| I would now like to come up with an approximation for each of 
| my digitized curves using a normal distribution, and obtain a measure of 
| how well the approximation fits the digitized points (some sort of R2).   

I would next ask if deviations from the putative normal form were best
modelled as absolute or relative (independent) errors.  If you are dealing
with a situation where the errors were relative and independent) you are in
luck.  Take the logs of the curve values, fit a quadratic regression (which
you can do with a very fast function in S if you set your mind to it) and
deduce your normal parameters from there.  If not, you may have a sticky
non-linear regression on your hands.

| The mean of a fitted normal curve would be constrained to match the peak
of 
| a digitized curve, so I guess it means solving for the best s.

I take it you mean the mean has to match the *position* of the peak, but
offhand I don't see why.  If you have sampling variation why is the postion
of the peak necessarily accurately determined but the shape at the peak
needs another 8 points around it?  Unless you have a good reason to do
otherwise, I would have thought that you would want to use all the
information to estimate both parameters.

Actually, if your curves are not normalized, you have three parameters:
mean, standard deviation and total mass, which correspond to (and are
non-linear functions of) the three parameters determining the quadratic.

| I'm not sure how to do this, and I'd sure appreciate it if 
| someone could point me in the right direction to complete my task.

We could if we knew more about the problem.  Questions like a sensible error
structure and whether or not it is positive with zero asymptotes are
crucial.  The above is of necessity a speculative response, so please use
with discretion.

Bill Venables.

messages.body_plain:
Yesterday I posted a question with a subject header "fitting a normal to a 
few digitized points?" and have been asked by Bill Venables for some more 
information crucial to addressing the problem.  In an effort to save anyone 
from having to follow a thread I am re-posting the original question with 
extra info added in square brackets.  I hope this provides sufficient extra 
information.  I appreciate very much any and all help.

I am using S+ 2000 R2 on Win98.

I have 1500 dome-shaped curves from a variety of simulations and empirical 
measurements (not mine).  For each curve I digitized the peak and four 
points on each side of the peak at specified proportions (> 50%) of the 
peak height.  [I say "dome-shaped" simply because I am dealing with the 
upper portion of the curves, where tails are far from obvious.  The 
original data are very much bell-shaped, and all values are positive.  The 
original curves all asymptote to zero on the left side, though many are 
truncated on the right.  Conceptually, it seems safe to assume that 
truncated curves would nevertheless asymptote to zero on the right.]

[For those that may be interested, the original data are from simulations 
and empirical measurements of fish habitat (area units) as a function of 
streamflow (volume per unit time).  That is, the data are not frequencies, 
but individual points.  Functionally, the curves are bell-shaped because 
zero water equals zero fish habitat, more water means more habitat up to 
some maximum, whereafter more water reduces available habitat by making it 
unsuitable (e.g., too fast).  Our project started with trying to predict 
the peak of these curves based on geographic and streamflow 
variables.  Having done a reasonable job of that, we now want to see if we 
can predict the shape of these curves.  Graphical explorations suggest the 
curves when plotted on a log scale can be well approximated (visually, at 
least) using a formula for the normal form.]

I would now like to come up with an approximation for each of my digitized 
curves using a normal distribution, and obtain a measure of how well the 
approximation fits the digitized points (some sort of R2).   The mean of a 
fitted normal curve would be constrained to match the peak of a digitized 
curve, so I guess it means solving for the best s.

[It seems safe to assume that deviations from the putative normal form can 
be modelled as independent errors.  Although there are three parameters to 
estimate, mean, standard deviation, and total mass, I thought I could 
simplify things by constraining the mean to match the position of the 
digitized curve, and scale the mass to match the scale of the digitized 
curve (percentage of peak height).  I am not committed to these simplifying 
assumptions.]

I'm not sure how to do this, and I'd sure appreciate it if someone could 
point me in the right direction to complete my task.

Thanks,

Todd Hatfield

messages.subject: analysis of paired comparison rating data
messages.subject_clean: analysis of paired comparison rating data
messages.body_plain:
I am looking for some guiding principles, sensitivity analysis, and

algorithms for the analysis of paired comparison rating data.  In

my data, each of n individuals make pairwise comparisons among

r alternatives on an interval scale.    For each of R=(r choose 2)

pairs, each individual is asked to rate his or her preference for

alternative i over alternative j on a scale -4 to 4 (say).   Thus the data

are structured as n x R matrix, or the upper triangular part of an n x r x 
r array.

If the interval scale is replaced by > / <, we could have data from
pairwise preference voting.

Could someone direct me please to a suite of Splus functions for
these type of data?    I say "suite of functions" because there are
plenty of choices for the analysis of pairwise preference voting data,
and there should be even more choices in analyzing pairwise comparison
rating data.    Since I'd like to make informed choices, and test
my choices empirically, I'd be interested in literature recommendations,
and thoughts on approaches to sensitivity analysis.

Thank you, Colin

At 11:42 AM 11-02-01 +1000, you wrote:
Hi Todd,

It looks as if you are dealing with lognormal densities.  I think the plan
that I naively outlined would be worth a try.  That is fit a quadratic
polynomial in log(x) to log(y).  Suppose the fitted function is

	log(y) = b0 + b1*log(x) + b2*log(x)^2

then mu = -b1/(2*b2) and sigma = sqrt(-1/(2*b2)).  The formula for the total
mass estimate is now simple in terms of b0, mu and sigma, but too fiddly to
type out here.

There are sampling problems with this if you want to get all finnicky about
the statistics (your measurements have not been random but with a view to
locating the maximum, &c) but from a numerical approximation point of view I
would not have any problems with it.  These are simulated curves, after all.

For software I would use the lmList function from the nlme library (now part
of S+2K, I believe, so it is just there.  This is a useful function for
fitting heaps of separate linear models all of the same form but you do need
to set you data up so that it can be accessed the way the function does it,
of course.

Regards,
Bill Venables.

messages.subject: RE: SPlus6 Java GUI extremely slow
messages.body_plain:
The usual cause of a slow Java GUI is running S-PLUS 6 on a remote machine,
and displaying on a local desktop using X Windows, across a slow network.
Remote Java applications transfer a large amount of information across a
network (much more than an equivalent X Windows application, for example),
and a slow network connection will result in slow painting of windows,
delayed creation of dialogs, etc.

Here are some tips for making the Java GUI run faster:

* Run S-PLUS on the local desktop machine.  (For example, a Linux machine
with XFree86 is particularly effective.)

* Run S-PLUS on a remote machine with a faster network connection to the
local machine

* Reduce the colour depth of the local display (say, from 32 or 16 bits to 8
bits).  This can dramatically reduce the quantity of information Java must
transmit over the network.

Further information is given in the S-LUS 6 Release Notes (see "Java Display
Issues").

# David Smith

messages.subject: Plot symbols for different factors
messages.body_plain:
Some time ago Bill Venables kindly helped me figure out a way to construct 
a bivariate scatterplot of grouped data so that different symbols and 
different colors were used for each group (factor) in the analysis.  Bill's 
suggestion involved a for loop, which works great, but requires 
considerably more effort than a simple one or two line command.

In R, I can do the following:

>attach(crabs)
>plot(FL, RW, type="n")
>points(FL, RW, pch=as.numeric(sp), col=as.numeric(sp))

OR in one step

>plot(FL, RW, pch=as.numeric(sp), col=as.numeric(sp))

Since S-Plus doesn't recycle the pch or col parameters, this fails with two 
errors:

> Too many values for parameter pch; some ignored
> Too many values for parameter col; some ignored

Is there some other way (short of an explicit loop) to accomplish in

messages.subject: trellis.par.set error - Summary
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks for Bill Dunlap, Nick Ellis, and Madeline Bauer who all pointed out
that you need to start trellis.device() before calling trellis.par.set():
==============================================
Here's Bill's solution:

If you don't explicitly start a graphics device then a device
gets started automatically when you ask to make a plot.  If
your first plot is a trellis plot, trellis.device() is called
to start the device.  If your first plot is not a trellis plot
then dev.start() is called and and the trellis parameters are
not attached to the .Device object.   trellis.par.get() can
handle that, but trellis.par.set() cannot.

E.g.,

> trellis.device()
>  superp <- trellis.par.get("superpose.line")
>  trellis.par.set("superpose.line", superp)
> # no problem

> dev.off()
 null device
           1
> plot(1:10)
> superp <- trellis.par.get("superpose.line")
> trellis.par.set("superpose.line", superp)
Problem in trellis.par.set: No data to interpret as logical value: if(p[i] !=
q[i]) stop("inconsistent component names")
Use traceback() to see the call stack

messages.subject: Re: deriv vs deriv3
messages.body_plain:
"Nick Ellis" <nick.ellis at marine.csiro.au> writes:

> D. M. Smith's deriv3() generates a function that returns an object
> containing a gradient attribute. The original deriv() also generates a
> gradient, but only if the following condition is satisfied
> 
> if(all(unlist(lapply(as.list(.actualArgs), is.name))))
> 
> (see below). I can't get this condition to be satisfied so I never get the
> derivative. Also, the if-block doesn't appear in the example in help(deriv).
> 
> Anyone know what what this undocumented if-block does? Should I avoid deriv
> and use deriv3 instead?

The purpose of the if-block is to get the column names of the gradient
to correspond to the actual parameter names, not the formal parameter
names, and also to protect against producing nonsensical gradient
arrays.

You can get the if condition to be satisfied by making sure
that you call the function with names for the actual parameters, not
with constant values.  (You can differentiate with respect to a
variable but you can't differentiate with respect to a constant.)

In your example you would use
 x <- -5; a <- 1; fun(x, a)

First the function checks that all the actual parameters are names
then it names the columns with the names by which it was called, not
the names under which it was defined.  Without that if-block, defining
the function as
 foo <- function(x, A, B, C) { ... }
and calling it as
 foo(x, b, c, a)
produces a gradient matrix with columns named "A", "B", and "C".

For safety, within functions like nls the column names of the gradient
matrix are used (if available) rather than the positions of the
columns to match columns to parameters.  For that we need the actual
parameter names not the formal parameter names.

messages.subject: ODBC: getting results into SQL Server database
messages.subject_clean: ODBC: getting results into SQL Server database
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I've found some very helpful info in the archives for using ODBC to
connect to my SQL Server database.
(In particular, I've found ways to make the OdbcConnection string and the
OdbcSqlQuery string.)
However, I've now run into some problems that the archives don't help me
solve.

The basic issue is that I have some results from a simulation that I want to
put into my database.  The
results are in a rather complex form, so I would rather not manually write
the insert statements,
but unfortunately, that's the only method I can get to work.  Below I show
the simple insert that works,
and two other methods that I would rather use and how they fail.

This simple method does work:
-------------------------------------------

1) Individual inserts

    sqlstr <- "INSERT INTO SIMRESULTS (CV_ID, MODEL_CLASS,
MODEL_CLASS_PARAM, WINDOW_NUM, VALUE) VALUES (199, 16, 11, 3, 53.0)"

    import.data(FileName="DataSvr",
     FileType="ODBC",
     DataFrame="out",

OdbcConnection="ODBC;DATABASE=DataSvr;UID=queen;PWD=blahblah;DSN=DataSvr",
     OdbcSqlQuery=sqlstr)

   (It is a bit ironic that to export data, I actually call the import
command!)

The following "better" methods, however, do not work:
----------------------------------------------------------------------------
---

2) Calling a stored procedure

   Since my results are rather complex, I actually want to parse them out
over several tables and run some cross-checks
   that everything "agrees".  For this reason, I would rather insert them by
calling a stored procedure I've written.  This
   makes the call look like this:

    sqlstr <- "EXEC FANCY_INSERT_PROCEDURE 199, 16, 11, 3, 53.0"

    import.data(FileName="DataSvr",
     FileType="ODBC",
     DataFrame="out",

OdbcConnection="ODBC;DATABASE=DataSvr;UID=queen;PWD=blahblah;DSN=DataSvr",
     OdbcSqlQuery=sqlstr)

   The problem is that sometimes this works fine.  But sometimes S-Plus
executes the stored procedure *twice*--
   or more precisely, what I see is the same data inserted twice into the
database.  I have not been able to isolate
   the conditions under which the data gets inserted once vs. when it gets
inserted twice.

   This is *not* the fault of the stored procedure.  I call the same
procedure via ODBC from two other applications
   to insert their simulation results (I want to compare their results with
S-Plus's results), but they have never
   inserted the data twice, although they have been used extensively.

3) Exporting a whole table

   Exporting the entire dataset as a SQL table would serve two purposes.
First, it would be a lot faster since I have
   many rows of data I want to move over.  Second, once the table is in the

messages.subject: Ridge regression
messages.body_plain:
The Design library handles penalized maximum likelihood estimation
for least squares and logistic models.  For least squares this is
ridge regression.  The ols function in Design does a decent job
in treating categorical predictors differently than continous
ones in scaling regression coefficients to put into the penalty
function.  ols also allows you to specify differential penalization
(e.g., penalize nonlinear interaction terms the most, followed
by linear interactions, followed by nonlinear main effects, then
minimally penalizing main linear effects).
--

Div. of Biostatistics & Epidem. Dept. of Health Evaluation Sciences
U. Virginia School of Medicine  http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat

messages.body_plain:
Hi S users.

I am generating an imaginary data set useing the following function:

y2<-function(n,w,v1,v2,v3,v4)
{
q<-c(1:n)
a<-c(0,cumsum(rexp(n-1)))
x.1<-matrix(0,n/w,w)
for(i in 1:n/w) x.1[i, ]<-sample(1:w,replace=F)
x.2<-t(x.1)
x.3<-as.numeric(x.2 > w/2)
e.1<- cumsum(c(v1,v2,v3,v4))
e.2<-as.vector(outer(a,e.1,"+"))
y<-as.vector(2+3*a+4*e.2+5*x.3)
assign( "df", data.frame(q=q,a=a,x.3=x.3,e.2=e.2,y=y), 0 )
return(df)
}

n-sample size
w-block size
vi-internal observation times in the imaginary study

x.3-treatment covariates using block randomisation

maximum likelihood method.  I have been told I can use NLMIN in  s-plus but

Note:

y<-as.vector(2+3*a+4*e.2+5*x.3)

cannot use lme.  Any help will be greatly appreciated.

messages.subject: Summary: rbind with a NULL data.frame
messages.subject_clean: Summary: rbind with a NULL data.frame
messages.body_plain:
Original post:
--------------
I'm interested in using rbind inside a loop and would like to somehow
intialize a data.frame to which I can rbind a row every iteration.  This
works with matrices, for example:

A_NULL
rbind(A, 1:5)

but I cannot make it work with data.frame.  

Solutions:
----------
1. Several people suggested creating a dummy row for the data.frame and then
deleting the row after the completion of the loop.

2. Bill Dunlap at Insightful came up with an almost perfect solution:

> A <- data.frame(One=numeric(0),
Two=factor(character(0),levels=c("No","Yes")))
> rbind(A, data.frame(One=pi, Two="Yes"))
       One Two
1 3.141593 Yes

If a person needs to avoid factors then you have to be clever, since 
> data.frame(One=numeric(0), Two=character(0))
does NOT allow rbind to work since S-Plus thinks Two is a factor.  
However, I came up with this twist:

  A <- data.frame(One=numeric(0), Two=character(0))
  A$Two_as.character(A$Two)
  rbind(A, data.frame(One=pi, Two="Yes"))

and Leonid Gibiansky discovered this (unintuitive) trick:

  A <- data.frame(a=numeric(0),b=double(0))
  rbind(A, data.frame(a=5,b="blue") )

Thanks to everyone,

Kevin

Kevin Wright, Research Scientist
Pioneer Hi-Bred Int'l, x4054.

messages.subject: Summary: Using C subroutine is Splus
messages.subject_clean: Summary: Using C subroutine is Splus
messages.body_plain:
I got several responses from Liaw, Andy; David Homiak; Shige Song; ROGER 
NGOUENET;Don MacQueen; and Xiaofei Wang. Many thanks to you guys help. 
Following 
is a summary of all the responses:
                    
Original Message:

Hello, S-users:

 I need to call a C subroutine in Splus simulations. As I just know a little 
 about C, this is hard to me. Can anyone  give me a simple example of how to do 
 this, including if I need to compile the C subroutine first and how to pass the

 parameters from the Splus function to the C subroutine. 

 Thanks and I appreciate your help,

 Jingli Song

 Dept. of Biostatistics
 Emory University

Suggestions:

1.Splus Programmer's guide. (Splus 2000 or splus5 or splus6) can be accessed 
online at ' www.insightful.com'.

2. Modern Applied Statistics with S-plus, (W.N. Venables and B. D. Ripley). 
There is an online resource of this book. the website is:
http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/MASS3/

3. S Programming(B. D. Ripley), website: 
http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/MASS3/Sprog/#OnLine
there also have availiable scripts file at:
http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/MASS3/Sprog/Sprog.zip

4. go to R website at: www.r-project.org

5. an brief introduction from David Homiak (with unix system).

   Then hopefully your unix system includes a C compiler. I believe most do.

   Here's a rough and partial outline.

   If I recall correctly, compile with the -o option (to get only an 
   object file output, you don't need or want to get an executable file).
   Put the output file in the same directory as the Splus function that 
   will call the C subroutine. Use the Splus CHAPTER command to make an 
   Splus shared object (should automatically get named S.so) from the C 
   object file. Actually, you may have to run the unix 'make' command 
   after the Splus CHAPTER command. Then, when you start Splus in that 
   directory, the C routine in S.so will be available.

   Then, you have to write an Splus function that calls the C 
   subroutine. I've done this with fortran, but not C so I can't help 
   you with some of the C stuff.

sets (on the order of 100 observations and 10 variables) that are related

idea for managing these data.  I would like to create something like a
by-object to store the data frame, status, results.  That way, I could
reference the data.frame by a statement like object["factor1",factor2"]$df.
This works in a test file that I have, but is rather slow.  Is there a
better way? a faster way?  What might be the limiting factors of this
approach?
  Thanks much.
Dave

messages.subject: SUMM: Assign() problem
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Prof. Ripley and Bert Gunter for answering my query.

Prof. Ripley points out that running a .ssc script effectively sources() 
it.  Because it needs to be able to back out if it fails, it uses quite a 
bit of memory.

He suggested using

  sqpe < foo.ssc > foo.out

which avoids all the build up (as will Splus /BATCH).

I used the assign() function instead of dbwrite(), because dbwrite seems to 
not properly write the object names, so I can't find them later, even after 
using synchronize(). dbwrite() seems to not wrtite the object names to the 
_nonfi file.

messages.subject: SUM: Help with BATCH (S+2000)
messages.body_plain:
First, my apologies for inadvertently sending a nonsensical post to the list 
while writing this summary.

Many thanks for all the rapid responses to my plea for help using S+ BATCH 
(initial message pasted at end). My problem was that while running simulations 
in BATCH mode I was frustrated by the unalterable display of a progress 
thermometer in the middle of my screen, on top of any other open applications! 
As it turns out there are several ways to get around this problem. Thanks to 
Andrea Spano & Pierre Duschene for the simplest fix; at the command line 
(Windows, not S+) use the following syntax:

Splus /BATCH_PROMPTS min /BATCH  infile.ssc outFile.txt errorFile.txt

I was not able to find any reference to the "min /BATCH" switch in the 
Programmer's Guide or the online help (Insightful Corp. people please take 
note) but this did the trick. That pesky progress thermometer was minimized in 
a corner of my screen, allowing other tasks to be completed while running 
simulations.

Other solutions are:

messages.subject: Annotated printing of arrays with named dimnames
messages.subject_clean: Annotated printing of arrays with named dimnames
messages.body_plain:
One aspect of S that bothers me (this applies to Version 5 for Unix, as well
as older versions that I still sometimes run) is that when printing matrices
or arrays there is no easy way to have labels for the dimensions printed
along with the labels for the levels of each dimension.  Because it is
possible to name the elements of the dimnames list, the data structures
necessary to support this type of labeling exist.  So, for example, when
printing the following simple matrix (whose structure below has been dumped
with dput())

matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4) , nrow = 2, ncol = 2
  dimnames = list("Fact1" = c("L1", "L2") , "Fact2" = c("L1", "L2") ) )

I would prefer output that looks like

           Fact2
           L1 L2
Fact1   L1  1  3
        L2  2  4

rather than the current default which is

   L1 L2
L1  1  3
L2  2  4

This approach is, I believe, upward compatible because most of the time the
dimnames components are not named and, in this case, the current default
output would presumably be produced.

Has anyone already come up with a way to do this?

Ted Wright

The Thomas C. Chalmers Centre for Systematic Reviews is a 
research initiative within the Children's Hospital of Eastern 
Ontario (CHEO) Research Institute, University of Ottawa, 
dedicated to producing evidence-based healthcare information. Our 
team includes clinicians, research methodologists, epidemiologists, 
statisticians, medical information specialists, project managers, and 
support staff. We value team work and offer an excellent 
mentorship program for an applied statistician career in health 
services research.  For more information about us, please visit our 
website at http://www.cheori.org/tcc.

approaches dealing with biased sampling in the synthesis of health 
research information (specifically, you will review and implement 
statistical methods dealing with selection bias in meta-analysis, 
conduct simulations to study their performance, and propose 
innovative ways for their dissemination.); and II. participate, with 
other members of the group, in providing statistical consulting 
services for clinicians in their research to improve the care of 
children in our hospital. 
    
Qualifications for the position include: a Masters or Ph.D. in 
statistics; working experience in statistical consulting; course work 
and hands-on experience in statistical computing and simulation;

messages.subject: panel.superpose solved
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Jim Pratt for a very quick solution. The problem was with colors
in 

xyplot(c14~silicate|Latfac,data=junkdf,
        layout=c(3,1),
        panel=function(x,y,...){
                panel.superpose(x,y,groups=Zfac,subscripts=T,
                        col=superpose.symbol$col,
                        pch=superpose.symbol$pch[1:4],
                        cex=superpose.symbol$cex)
                abline(-70,-1,lwd=2)
                })

not being set correctly for Zfac in the subplots.

The solution is:

xyplot(c14~silicate|Latfac,data=junkdf,
        layout=c(3,1),
        groups=Zfac,
        panel=function(x,y,...){
                abline(-70,-1,lwd=2)
                panel.superpose(x,y,
                        col=superpose.symbol$col,
                        pch=superpose.symbol$pch[1:4],
                        cex=superpose.symbol$cex,...)
                })

messages.subject: Graphics driver speeds
messages.body_plain:
This is a problem for which I am afraid there is no (current) 
solution--but if there is one, I would very much appreciate hearing 
about it.

The new java-based graphics drivers are very slow compared to the 
older non-jave drivers. Here is some output to show this. For 
example, in this run, creating a PNG file took 254 times as long 
(elapsed time) as a PDF file. Most of the time appears to be used 
during the execution of dev.off().

Source code that created the matrix of times is given below.

            usr  sys elapsed child.usr child.sys
 pdf.time  0.10 0.00    0.18      0.00      0.00
 eps.time  0.28 0.07    1.17      0.12      0.29
  ps.time  0.30 0.05    1.30      0.16      0.32
jpeg.time 14.02 0.04   18.20      0.00      0.00
 png.time 35.93 0.06   45.80      0.00      0.00

Note:
>  version
Version 6.0 Release 1 for Sun SPARC, SunOS 5.6 : 2000

----- Source code ------
ps.time <- unix.time({
  postscript("foo.ps", onefile = T, print.it = F)
  plot(1:3)
  dev.off()
})

eps.time <- unix.time({
  postscript("foo.eps", onefile = F, print.it = F)
  plot(1:3)
  dev.off()
})

pdf.time <- unix.time({
  pdf.graph("foo.pdf", width = 6, height = 4)
  plot(1:3)
  dev.off()
})

jpeg.time <- unix.time({
  java.graph("foo.jpeg", format = "")
  plot(1:3)
  dev.off()
})

png.time <- unix.time({
  java.graph("foo.png", format = "PNG")
  plot(1:3)
  dev.off()
})

names(pdf.time) <- c("usr", "sys", "elapsed", "child.usr", "child.sys")
drvr.times <- rbind(pdf.time, eps.time, ps.time, jpeg.time, png.time)

print(drvr.times)
--

Don MacQueen

Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
Livermore, CA, USA

messages.subject: RE: Graphics driver speeds
messages.body_plain:
I checked with the S-PLUS development team (thanks, Michael!) on this issue.
Unfortunately, it seems there is no easy solution here.  The bitmap file
writing ("JPEG", "TIFF", "PNG", "PNM", or "BMP) is all done in the Java
"Advanced Imaging" package.  S-PLUS calls into this package to create a jpeg
(png, etc) driver, and draw to it.  If the Java folks ever make faster
versions of
these routines, we will of course include them in S-PLUS.

Postscript and pdf files are created quickly as they call internal C code
written by Insightful.

Incidentally, the reason that all of the time is under dev.off() is that
none of the file writing is done until the device is closed: at this point,
the current graphics commands are drawn to the file.

# David Smith

messages.subject: How to make Splus wait
messages.body_plain:
The short version of the query: 
Splus takes a while to execute a call to a function that includes compiled
FORTRAN code. How can one make Splus delay the execution of the next Splus
command until the function is done?

Some details:
MART is a data mining tool that was ipmlemented in Splus by J. Friedman
(jhf at stat.stanford.edu). In single runs, MART works fine. I'd like to
automate running MART repeatedly with no human supervision. Unfortunately,
MART does not provide a visible return code for signaling run completion to
Splus so that if other commands follow the call to MART, Splus will start
them without waiting for files generated by the last MART run, and the next
command will fail, or fail to execute properly. 

Users have no direct access to the parts of the MART routines that are
written in FORTRAN. 

I am running the current release of MART using Splus2000 on one computer
under Windows 95 and on another under Windows 98.
